passage: Team lead's note, Friday. I'm Asif, and this week I watched how Parul spends the evenings. Manav starts tasks with real energy: the vendor list, the price comparison, the customer follow-up. Each one is left about eighty percent finished. Parul has been quietly chasing the vendors, correcting the price sheet and sending the follow-up mails, and twice stayed until eight. Parul did not complain, only said, “It's fine, it needs doing.” Manav has no idea this is happening. What I did next: I asked at Monday's meeting who owns each task until it is closed, and wrote a name beside every line. Then I told Parul privately that the evenings would not be covered again.

passage: Thursday. Another late one. Uma is wonderful at starting things: yesterday she launched the new event checklist with such energy that everyone was excited. By afternoon it had six open items: two suppliers not confirmed, the seating list incomplete, one invitation unsent. I noticed them because I had promised the client an update. So I called the suppliers, finished the list and sent the invitation, which took my whole evening. Nobody has asked me to. I don't want to complain about Uma, because she's not lazy and the ideas are good. But my own work slid to tomorrow, and I keep feeling a low hum of resentment I don't quite want. Maybe the checklist needs a name against each item. — Darshan

passage: I'm Pooja, and for a year I sat next to Damini at the marketing agency. Damini is brilliant at starts. She'd pitch an idea on Monday, draft half the slides by Tuesday and then be onto something new. The loose ends came to me. I'd find her half-written client email in the shared folder at six and finish it. I'd chase the printer for the brochure she'd ordered and forgotten. Nobody noticed. Our manager praised Damini's energy at the review. I went home and cried in the auto, tired and invisible. The next week I made a shared tracker with an owner for every task, including hers. It helped, a little.

qa.q: What did Pooja find in the shared folder at six?
qa.a: Pooja found a half-written client email.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling in the auto after the review?
qa.a: Pooja felt tired, invisible and hurt that the praise went to Damini's energy while the finishing work went unseen.

qa.q: What did Pooja try, and why could it help?
qa.a: A shared tracker with an owner for every task, which makes loose ends visible and puts them back with the person who started them.

qa.q: How might Damini see her own work habits?
qa.a: Damini probably sees herself as energetic and productive, with no idea of the chasing and finishing that happens after she moves on.

grounding: A worker describes quietly finishing the loose ends of a colleague who starts brightly but does not close tasks.

passage:
Supervisor's note, IT support desk, end of quarter.
I've noticed a pattern I should have caught sooner. Divyansh opens tickets quickly and gives users a cheerful first reply. But many of his tickets stay half-resolved, and Gautam has been closing them, often after hours. This month Gautam closed fourteen tickets that Divyansh had opened. When I asked Gautam about it, he looked at the floor and said, "Someone has to." He sounded worn out, not proud. Divyansh seemed genuinely surprised when I showed him the list. Next step: from Monday, every ticket stays with the person who opens it until closed, and I'll check the list each Friday.

qa.q: How many tickets did Gautam close that Divyansh had opened?
qa.a: Gautam closed fourteen tickets that Divyansh had opened.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he said, "Someone has to"?
qa.a: He felt worn out and quietly resentful, looking at the floor rather than sounding proud.

qa.q: What change did the supervisor make, and how could it help?
qa.a: Every ticket now stays with whoever opens it until closed, with a Friday check, so the hidden work stops falling on Gautam.

qa.q: How did Divyansh react when shown the list?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed genuinely surprised, since the cost of his half-finished tickets had been invisible to him.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows how one colleague quietly finishes another's loose ends, and the cost of that invisible work.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Did Nilesh's work again today. He started the vendor comparison sheet last week, very excited, filled in three suppliers and then left for a conference. Our manager asked for it at four. I finished the other five suppliers by seven. Nilesh texted "thanks yaar, you're a lifesaver 😊" and that was it.
I'm not angry at him exactly. He means well. But this is the fourth time this month, and I'm the one missing dinner. I feel used, and a bit stupid for not saying anything.
Tomorrow I'm going to tell him, calmly, that he needs to close what he opens, or hand it over properly.
Shalini

qa.a: He filled in three suppliers.

qa.q: What is Shalini feeling after finishing the sheet?
qa.a: Shalini feels used and a bit stupid for staying quiet, though not exactly angry at Nilesh.

qa.a: To tell Nilesh calmly that he must close what he opens or hand it over properly, which names the problem without an attack.

qa.q: How does Nilesh seem to see the situation?
qa.a: Nilesh seems grateful but unaware, sending a cheerful thanks without noticing that this is the fourth time Shalini has covered.
